name: Pinguecula / pterygium removal

card.summary: Surgery to remove the yellowish or pinkish conjunctival growths of pinguecula and pterygium, done mainly for medical reasons and sometimes for looks.
card.aka: Pterygium excision, pterygium surgery, surfer's eye surgery
card.note: Pterygium can recur after surgery, so technique and follow-up matter in the published studies.

quick.overview:
A pinguecula is a yellowish bump on the white of the eye, and a pterygium is a related fleshy, often pink growth that extends onto the cornea. Both are linked to long-term sun and dust exposure. Removal is a recognised eye operation, mostly for vision, irritation or contact lens problems, and some people seek it for cosmetic reasons.

The surgical literature is large for pterygium and focuses on recurrence rates, techniques and effects on corneal shape. Pinguecula removal has far less published research.
quick.mechanism: The growth is surgically excised. Modern techniques usually cover the bare area with tissue, most often a conjunctival autograft from the same eye, held with sutures or tissue glue, to reduce regrowth. Other approaches in the literature include amniotic membrane, mitomycin C and, historically, beta irradiation.
quick.risks: Recurrence is the main reported problem, with rates varying widely by technique and population; an encyclopedic summary says about half of cases recur, while grafting studies report lower figures. Other documented issues include corneal astigmatism changes and complications of adjunct treatments such as radiation.

lead: A pinguecula is a yellowish raised area of the conjunctiva, and a pterygium is a related triangular growth that extends from the conjunctiva onto the cornea. Both are associated with ultraviolet light and dust exposure; a pterygium is sometimes called surfer's eye [1][2].

Removal is typically considered when a pterygium affects vision through astigmatism or scarring, causes persistent irritation or contact lens intolerance, or is cosmetically bothersome. Many cases need no surgery, and artificial tears are commonly used for irritation [1][3].

The surgical literature has examined techniques such as bare sclera excision, conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, mitomycin C and radiation, with recurrence as the central outcome [3][4][5].

paras: A pterygium is a benign growth of conjunctiva onto the cornea, often starting on the nasal side. Its exact cause is unknown, but UV exposure, dust and genetic factors are implicated, and prevalence varies from about 1% to 33% depending on region [1].
A pinguecula has similar histology but stays on the conjunctiva and does not extend onto the cornea [1].

Bare sclera excision leaves the exposed area uncovered. Conjunctival autografting covers it with tissue from the same eye, and amniotic membrane transplantation is an alternative in extensive cases [1][6]. Extended removal followed by extended conjunctival transplantation has been studied for both primary and recurrent pterygium, including its cosmetic result [7][8]. Sliding conjunctival flaps have also been described [9]. Fixation with sutures or fibrin glue and the adjunct mitomycin C are subjects of comparison trials [10][11].

In an early randomised trial in the Caribbean, recurrence was 21% in 19 grafted cases versus 37% in 16 bare sclera cases, a difference that was not statistically significant, and younger age was strongly associated with recurrence [6]. A review of 161 recurrences examined how long patients must be followed to capture recurrence [12]. A long-term series of beta irradiation after removal reported recurrence and complications over more than a decade of follow-up [13].

A Cochrane review summarised in an encyclopedic source found autograft less likely to recur at six months than amniotic membrane transplant, while the effect of adding mitomycin C was unclear [1]. A 2021 review notes that pterygium can induce corneal irregularity and astigmatism and that removal can change refractive properties [3].

Clinical research is substantial for pterygium surgery, including randomised and prospective studies of recurrence [6][7][8] and registered trials comparing mini-SLET with limbal-conjunctival autograft [14], sutured versus sutureless autograft [15], glue versus sutures [10], and mitomycin C with amniotic membrane [11]. Studies of corneal effects include analyses of astigmatism induced by pterygium [16][17] and a registered trial of topographic changes after surgery [18]. No studies found specifically addressed cosmetic-only removal of a pinguecula.

timeline.event: First reported randomised trial of conjunctival autografting for pterygium [6].
Long-term results of beta irradiation after pterygium removal published [13].
Prospective study of extended removal with extended conjunctival transplantation [8].
